title: My game is really starting to come together... turn-based rpg game GodScar
author: irbrandonl
selftext:
Things are really starting to come together with GodScar!

Just wanted to share another little preview of my turn-based RPG. This video shows a bit of everything I've been working on, from the world and environments to the art direction, battle system, animations, and more.

There's still a ton of work to be done and plenty of things I want to improve, but it's been pretty cool seeing everything slowly come together.

For anyone curious, I'm currently using Godot, Claude Opus 5.5 (Extra Effort or higher), and Blender for some of the more complex 3D models. I've had a few people ask about my workflow, so if you're curious about how I'm making certain things, feel free to ask. I'm always happy to share what I've learned.

Also, a few people have been asking how they can follow the game's development. I'm planning to get a Discord set up sometime today so I can share more updates, get feedback, and keep everyone in the loop.

I'm also looking for people who might be interested in playtesting once the demo is ready. If that's something you'd like to be part of, just leave a comment or shoot me a DM!

As always, let me know what you guys think. I appreciate all the feedback and support so far. It's genuinely been helping me make the game better.

replies.author: irbrandonl
replies.body:
Thank you! I've actually been waiting for someone to ask specifically about the 2D sprite pipeline because, out of everything I've worked on, this was probably one of the most difficult things to get right.

I won't go through every failed attempt unless you're interested in hearing about those, but I'll share what I think finally worked for me.

First, references are extremely important. I went through several sprite sheets I found online, specifically looking for ones that included full animation sets and matched the general art style I was going for. I then provided those to Claude as references and gave it detailed instructions on what I wanted.

Second, use Ultracode with at least Extra Effort. This was probably the biggest difference maker for me. I know Ultracode gets a lot of criticism because of how expensive it is and how many agents it uses, but personally, I'd rather spend more on a serious attempt than repeatedly burn through lower-effort requests that don't get me anywhere.

Even then, don't expect everything to work on the first try.

The animations are where things get really frustrating. You might get a sprite that looks great, but the moment it starts moving, you'll notice all kinds of problems. This is where you really have to be specific with your feedback. Tell Claude exactly what's working, what's broken, what needs to change, and which references it should go back to. Simply telling it that the animation looks bad usually isn't enough.

And even with all that, I still think there's a fair amount of luck involved.

I've helped several people try to replicate my results, and unfortunately, some still haven't been able to get theirs working properly. I think I went through more than 10 Ultracode requests myself before I finally got something I was happy with. It was a constant cycle of telling Claude to change this, fix that, reference this animation, adjust that movement, etc.

One interesting thing I've noticed, though, is that Opus 5.5 seems to handle monster sprites significantly better than humanoid sprites. I'm not entirely sure why, but most of my monster sprites came out pretty well on the first attempt. Humanoid sprites, on the other hand, were a completely different story.

So yeah, I wish I had a straightforward process I could guarantee would work for everyone, but I don't. Good references, detailed instructions, Ultracode, and a lot of patience are what eventually got me there. Even then, there's still some trial and error involved, especially with humanoid animations.

replies.author: irbrandonl
replies.body:
Thank you! I really appreciate that. And yeah, I'm more than happy to share what I've learned because I know how frustrating it can be to get it right... 

So I'll actually start from the beginning because I think that might help explain how I got to where I am now.

When I first started GODSCAR, I used Claude Opus 5.5 on Ultracode and essentially told it that I wanted to create a turn-based RPG with the same HD-2D art style as Octopath Traveler. That was really my starting point. I wanted the combination of detailed 3D environments, 2D character sprites, atmospheric lighting, and the overall visual presentation that makes those games stand out.

From there, I started building on that foundation and refining things individually. I think that's an important distinction because I didn't necessarily create the entire visual pipeline from scratch myself. I gave Claude a clear direction for the style I wanted, let it establish the initial foundation, and then worked on improving everything from there.

As far as the 3D assets go, I use a few different approaches depending on what I'm trying to accomplish. Most of my development is still done through Claude Code, specifically Opus 5.5 on Extra Effort or Ultracode, but I also use Blender for more complex 3D models, especially the colossal monsters. I've experimented with Tripo AI as well, and I think it's a pretty good alternative for generating assets, particularly ones that don't require complicated animations. It can also be more cost-effective in the long run.

One thing that's made a huge difference for me is providing detailed visual references. I rarely just ask Claude to create something without giving it an idea of exactly what I'm looking for. I'll find references online or generate concept images using Codex, then use those to guide the modeling, textures, materials, proportions, and overall appearance.

For animations and cinematic sequences, I primarily have Claude handle those directly inside Godot. This includes camera movements, particle effects, attack animations, environmental interactions, and transitions. The biggest thing I've learned here is to break everything down rather than asking it to do too much at once.

For example, when working on one of my colossal monsters, I'll usually focus on getting the model right first, then its movement and animations, followed by the attacks and visual effects. I used to let Claude tackle everything at once, but that caused a lot of problems because I'd end up with a decent-looking model that moved terribly or had attacks that didn't visually connect with the creature.

I've also started establishing predefined workflows for Claude to follow. Instead of immediately implementing everything, I'll have it review references, explain what it's planning to do, create a small working example, and then wait for my feedback before moving forward. That's been incredibly helpful, especially when dealing with more complicated systems or assets.

And to answer your question about vibe coding, yes, a large portion of what I'm doing would fall into that category. I'm not manually creating every model or writing every line of code myself. But there's also a lot more involved than simply asking Claude to make something and accepting the first result.

I'm constantly reviewing footage, identifying things that look wrong, giving detailed feedback, and having Claude make adjustments. Sometimes that takes two or three attempts, and other times it takes well over ten. My humanoid sprite animations were probably one of the most frustrating examples of that.

So if I had to simplify my process, it's basically establish the visual foundation → gather references → give detailed instructions → create the assets → integrate everything into Godot → work on animations and VFX → review and refine until I'm satisfied.

I definitely wouldn't say I've figured everything out, and there's still a lot of trial and error involved. But I think the biggest thing that's helped me is learning how to give Claude very specific direction instead of relying on it to figure everything out on its own.

Hopefully that gives you a better idea of how I've been approaching things! If there's a specific part you want me to go into more detail about, I'm happy to share what I can.

By that, I mean generic things and ideas AI will provide for you. You should be leading the AI not the other way around, and that is what the anti-AI crowd will point at and get hung up about. Here's just a few:

- monsters are all in different styles, some are 3D models others are pixel art. 
- Is each attack move going to be a cutscene? simplicity and combat speed is important, it doesn't have to be self indulgent cut scene after cut scene. 
- the game looks like every HD-2D game spit out by AI. I know because in your first town the fountain has water going up and not down, just like every iteration of this same village claude has spit out.

- The name "GodScar". On one hand, I applaud you for not choosing the first AI give name of "GodFall" or "EmberScar", but still it's an obvious lame AI 2 cool sounding words jammed together.

replies.author: irbrandonl
replies.body:
Thanks for the detailed feedback! I appreciate you taking the time to go through everything. I'll try to address each of your points below...

**"Monsters are all in different styles, some are 3D models, others are pixel art."**

A couple of other people have brought this up as well, so I'm happy to explain the reasoning behind it.

I currently have over 100 different monsters in the game, with around 8–10 being fully 3D models, and more still in development. The 3D models are primarily reserved for bosses, specifically what I call my colossal monsters. The other 90 or so monsters are 2D sprites, which also include some bosses.

My original thought was to make these much larger encounters feel more impactful by giving them fully animated 3D models, more elaborate attacks, and a stronger sense of scale.

That being said, I've definitely considered going with a more traditional HD-2D approach and keeping all monsters as sprites for the sake of visual consistency. It's still a real possibility, and I haven't completely made up my mind on it yet.

**"Is each attack move going to be a cutscene? Simplicity and combat speed is important."**

No, definitely not. The more cinematic attacks you're seeing are part of what I consider the Ultimate tier.

Each job has at least one Ultimate ability alongside several other regular attacks and skills that don't involve cutscenes. I agree that combat pacing is extremely important, especially in a turn-based RPG where players will be fighting hundreds of battles throughout the game.

The goal is to make those bigger abilities feel special without turning every encounter into a series of lengthy animations.

**"The game looks like every HD-2D game spit out by AI. The fountain has water going up and not down."**

The fountain issue has actually been pointed out already, and it's currently queued to be fixed as part of my ongoing environment improvements.

As far as the environments looking too similar to other AI-generated HD-2D games, I'd genuinely be interested in hearing more specific examples of what you're referring to.

I'm not dismissing the criticism because visual identity is something I want GODSCAR to have, and if there are areas that feel too generic or repetitive, I'd like to address them.

I do want to emphasize, though, that everything being shown is still alpha footage. A lot of the environments, assets, animations, and effects are actively being improved, so what you're seeing isn't necessarily representative of the final product.

**"The music is straight Suno's 'make me an RPG battle theme.'"**

I can understand this criticism to an extent. Suno does have a certain recognizable sound, and I think some of that can be difficult to avoid regardless of how much direction you give it.

But I do want to clarify that I'm not simply typing something like "make me an RPG battle theme" and using whatever comes out.

For most of the music, I provide pretty detailed direction regarding the tone, atmosphere, musical style, instrumentation, and even lyrics when they're applicable.

I'll usually generate around six different variations based on the same general direction, make adjustments to the style, and then choose the one I think fits the scene best.

Obviously, that doesn't mean everyone is going to like the results, and that's completely fair. Music is subjective, and I'm still evaluating what works best for the game. I just wanted to clarify that there's a bit more thought going into the process than a simple one-line prompt.

**"The name GODSCAR sounds like two cool AI-generated words jammed together."**

This one actually made me laugh a little because GODSCAR is one of the things I came up with entirely on my own.

The name has a pretty significant connection to the game's lore, particularly the gods, their origins, and the events that have shaped the world.

I can understand why someone might think it sounds like an AI-generated fantasy title, and you're certainly entitled to think it's corny, but the name itself wasn't generated by AI.

There's a specific reason I chose it, and that meaning will become clearer as players experience the story.

Again, thanks for taking the time to share all of this!This was a great response!

I know not everyone is going to agree with the direction I'm taking, and that's perfectly fine. I'm sharing these development updates partly because I want to hear different perspectives and identify things I might be overlooking.

I'm not against criticism at all, especially when it gives me something specific I can work on. So if you have any other suggestions or examples of things you think could be improved, feel free to share them. I'm always open to hearing more.
